content.title: About
content.content: Beef roast is a cooked cut of beef, usually a rib roast, sirloin or chuck, prepared by searing at high heat to form a crust and then slowly roasting to the desired doneness. It offers a rich, meaty flavor, tender texture, and a distinctive aroma created by the Maillard reaction of proteins and fats.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The term “roast beef” dates back to medieval England and has become a classic British dish.
Traditionally, roast beef is sliced thin and served cold as a sandwich filling or appetizer.
In the United Kingdom, roast beef is considered a national staple and often appears on Sunday dinner tables.
Proper cooking creates a crispy outer crust while keeping the interior juicy and pink.
Marinating briefly in salt, herbs, and a touch of acid (like vinegar) can enhance tenderness.

items.title: High‑quality protein
items.content: Beef provides all essential amino acids needed for muscle growth and tissue repair.

items.title: Rich in iron
items.content: Heme iron from beef is highly bioavailable and supports healthy hemoglobin levels.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Roast beef is a good source of B12, niacin (B3) and riboflavin (B2), which are important for energy metabolism.

items.title: Zinc
items.content: Zinc in beef helps maintain immune function and wound healing.

items.title: Creatine
items.content: Creatine supports strength and endurance during physical activity.

items.title: Saturated fat content
items.content: Excessive intake may raise cholesterol levels.

items.title: Nitrites and carcinogens at high temperatures
items.content: Very high‑heat cooking can produce harmful compounds if done frequently.

items.title: Beef allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to beef.

items.title: Digestive discomfort
items.content: Large portions of heavy red meat can cause stomach upset in sensitive people.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Slice roast beef thinly and serve hot or cold. It works well in salads, sandwiches, wraps, tacos, and as a pizza topping. Let the meat rest 10‑15 minutes after cooking for juicier slices.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep cooked roast beef in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. For longer storage, freeze it tightly sealed for up to 3 months. Discard if it develops an off‑odor or discoloration.

content.title: About
content.content: Bread stuffing made with egg is a ready‑to‑eat product consisting of finely diced bread mixed with beaten eggs and seasonings. It is commonly used as a filling for pies, casseroles, and sandwiches. During preparation the bread absorbs the egg mixture, resulting in a soft, flavorful, and nutritious filling.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Traditionally this stuffing was made at home to make use of leftover bread crumbs.
In some regions finely chopped onion or fresh herbs are added for extra aroma.
The combination of bread and egg provides a quick source of energy from carbohydrates and protein.
The stuffing can be kept in the refrigerator for up to 3 days and frozen for up to 2 months.
Variations may include cheese, ham, or vegetables.

items.title: Rich source of protein
items.content: Eggs provide a complete protein containing all essential amino acids, important for tissue repair.

items.title: Energy value
items.content: Carbohydrates from bread together with fats from eggs deliver sustained satiety.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Eggs contain vitamin B12, riboflavin and niacin, supporting metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: The stuffing supplies iron, phosphorus and selenium, which are vital for blood formation and antioxidant protection.

items.title: Easy to digest
items.content: Warm texture and soft consistency aid quick digestion.

items.title: Egg allergy
items.content: People allergic to eggs may experience reactions ranging from mild to anaphylactic after consumption.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: When salt is added, monitor the amount to stay within daily sodium recommendations.

items.title: Shelf life
items.content: Because of the eggs, the product spoils quickly if not stored properly; keep it refrigerated.

items.title: Bacterial contamination
items.content: Improper cooking of eggs can allow salmonella growth.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Use the stuffing as a filling for puff pastries, casseroles, sandwiches, or serve it as a hot side dish. Heat in the oven or on a skillet until golden before serving.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store in an airtight container in the refrigerator at 0‑4 °C for no more than 3 days. For longer storage freeze in a freezer‑safe bag for up to 2 months. Reheat thoroughly before consumption.

content.title: About
content.content: Broccoli, frozen, cooked with oil (4412) is a ready‑to‑eat vegetable product made from fresh broccoli that is quickly frozen and then sautéed in vegetable oil. It retains most of its nutrients, has a tender texture and a light fried‑oil aroma.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Broccoli belongs to the cruciferous family and is rich in vitamins B, C and K.
Freezing immediately after harvest preserves over 90 % of vitamin C.
Sautéing in oil creates a small amount of beneficial carotenoids, enhancing antioxidant activity.
While common in Asian cuisine, frozen broccoli is convenient for soups, stews and pasta dishes.
One package (≈300 g) provides more than 30 % of the daily vitamin C requirement for an adult.

items.title: Rich in vitamin C
items.content: Vitamin C supports the immune system and aids collagen synthesis.

items.title: Contains dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber promotes healthy digestion and helps maintain satiety.

items.title: Source of folate
items.content: Folate is essential for cell division and especially important during pregnancy.

items.title: Provides antioxidants
items.content: Glucosinolates and carotenoids help protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Low‑calorie food
items.content: A single serving contains about 80 kcal, making it suitable for weight‑management diets.

items.title: Cruciferous vegetable allergy
items.content: A small number of people may experience an allergic reaction to broccoli.

items.title: Oil content
items.content: The product is cooked in oil, so those monitoring fat intake should consider its calories.

items.title: Additive presence
items.content: Some manufacturers may add preservatives; check the label if you are sensitive to food additives.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Heat the frozen broccoli in the microwave, on a skillet, or add it directly to soups, stews, pasta or rice dishes. Serve as a side dish or incorporate into salads after cooling.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep frozen at –18 °C (0 °F) or lower. After opening, use within 3–4 days while maintaining a consistent cold chain. Do not thaw and refreeze the product.

content.title: About
content.content: Chicken or turkey with stuffing is a whole piece of poultry that is filled with a mixture of bread, herbs, vegetables, and sometimes meat. The dish is traditionally roasted in the oven until the skin turns golden, resulting in juicy meat and a flavorful stuffing.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Stuffing often includes breadcrumbs, onion, celery, and spices, which keep the meat moist and aromatic.
In the United States, stuffing turkey for Thanksgiving dates back to the colonial era.
Chicken with stuffing is popular in European cuisines, especially in Germany and Poland, where rice or buckwheat may be used.
During roasting, juices from the stuffing seep into the meat, enhancing flavor and texture.
The dish is commonly served with a gravy made from the pan drippings.

items.title: High‑quality protein
items.content: Poultry provides complete protein essential for muscle growth and tissue repair.

items.title: Low in saturated fat (especially turkey)
items.content: Chicken and turkey contain less saturated fat than red meat, supporting heart health.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Meat supplies niacin, vitamin B6 and B12, which aid metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: Poultry is a source of selenium, zinc and phosphorus, important for immunity and bone health.

items.title: Fiber from the stuffing
items.content: When whole‑grain bread, vegetables, or legumes are added to the stuffing, the dish gains extra dietary fiber for digestive health.

items.title: Food‑borne illness risk
items.content: Improper cooking can leave bacteria such as Salmonella; the internal temperature should reach 165 °F (74 °C).

items.title: High sodium in prepared stuffing
items.content: Store‑bought mixes often contain salt and soy sauce; people with hypertension should monitor intake.

items.title: Allergy to stuffing ingredients
items.content: Stuffing may contain nuts, dairy, or gluten, requiring caution for allergic individuals.

items.title: Calorie density
items.content: Combining meat with a rich stuffing can increase calories; portion control is advised.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Preheat the oven to 350 °F (180 °C). Prepare stuffing by mixing breadcrumbs, finely chopped vegetables, herbs and spices. Gently loosen the skin of the bird, fill with stuffing, and secure with kitchen twine or toothpicks. Roast for 1.5–2 hours, basting occasionally with pan juices. Serve with roasted vegetables and gravy.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Cool leftovers to room temperature, then place in an airtight container. Refrigerate for up to 3 days. For longer storage, freeze in freezer‑safe bags for up to 2 months. Reheat to an internal temperature of 165 °F (74 °C) before serving.

content.title: About
content.content: Pizzelle are traditional Italian wafer‑like cookies shaped like delicate cones. The dough is made from eggs, sugar, butter, flour and flavorings (commonly vanilla or lemon zest). It is rolled thin and baked in a special patterned iron, producing crisp, aromatic shells with a characteristic lattice design.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Pizzelle originate from the Abruzzo region, where they are prepared for holidays and family celebrations.
They are traditionally dusted with powdered sugar, honey, jam, or chocolate drizzle.
Many dough variations exist: classic butter, gluten‑free, cocoa‑infused, or nut‑enhanced versions.
In Italy pizzelle are often used as a base for ice‑cream sandwiches, with a scoop of gelato placed between two shells.
The name “pizzelle” derives from the Italian “pizzicare,” meaning “to pinch,” referring to their crisp bite.

items.title: Energy source
items.content: The carbohydrate content provides a quick source of energy, useful before physical activity.

items.title: Small amount of protein
items.content: Eggs and dairy in the batter add a modest amount of protein that supports tissue repair.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Flour and eggs contain B1, B2 and B6 vitamins, which play roles in energy metabolism.

items.title: Calcium
items.content: Butter and eggs contribute calcium, important for bone and teeth health.

items.title: Antioxidants from flavorings
items.content: Vanilla, lemon zest or cinnamon add antioxidant compounds that help protect cells.

items.title: Gluten allergy
items.content: Traditional recipes use wheat flour, making pizzelle unsuitable for people with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity.

items.title: Dairy allergy
items.content: Butter may trigger reactions in individuals with lactose intolerance or milk protein allergy.

items.title: High sugar content
items.content: Added sugar increases calorie count and can contribute to tooth decay when consumed frequently.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: Pizzelle are relatively calorie‑dense; moderate portion sizes are recommended for weight management.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Pizzelle can be enjoyed as a sweet snack on their own, dusted with powdered sugar, drizzled with honey, jam or chocolate. They are often used as a base for ice‑cream sandwiches, added to dessert salads, or used as decorative elements on cakes.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store pizzelle in an airtight container in a cool, dry place. For longer shelf life keep them in the refrigerator to maintain crispness. Discard any that become soft, stale or develop an off‑odor.

content.title: About
content.content: Corn grits are a coarsely ground meal made from dried corn kernels. They are cooked into a thick porridge that can be creamy or firm. In the United States this dish is called grits and is especially loved in the South, while in Moldova and Romania it is made into mămăligă. Corn grits have a mild, slightly sweet flavor and come in yellow or white.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Grits are a traditional dish of the American South that came from Native American cooking.
Mămăligă is a national dish of Moldovans and Romanians, and in Georgia, corn meal is made into gomi.
Grits come in whole-grain and quick-cooking forms, and their cooking times differ greatly.
Hominy is corn treated with an alkali, after which the niacin in it is better absorbed.
Corn is naturally gluten-free.

items.title: Source of energy
items.content: Corn grits provide carbohydrates that are quickly turned into energy.

items.title: Contain carotenoids
items.content: Yellow corn contains lutein and zeaxanthin, which are important for eye health.

items.title: Contain fiber
items.content: Whole-grain grits provide more fiber.

items.title: Suitable for gluten-free diets
items.content: Pure corn grits can be part of a gluten-free diet when properly labeled.

items.title: Fortified with vitamins
items.content: Some types of grits are fortified with iron and B vitamins.

items.title: High glycemic index
items.content: Quick grits raise blood sugar faster than whole-grain grits; people with diabetes should watch their portion.

items.title: Monotonous diet
items.content: A diet based mostly on corn that is not alkali-treated, and lacking other foods, used to lead to pellagra, a niacin deficiency.

items.title: Gluten
items.content: People with celiac disease should choose grits labeled gluten-free because of possible cross-contamination.

items.title: Mold and mycotoxins
items.content: Corn stored poorly may contain mycotoxins; discard grits that are moldy or smell musty.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Cook grits in water or milk in a ratio of about 1 to 4, stirring for 20–30 minutes until thickened; whole-grain grits take longer. Season the porridge with salt and add butter, cheese, or herbs. Cooled firm porridge can be sliced and baked or fried.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store grits in an airtight container in a dry, cool, dark place. Whole-grain grits with the germ are best kept in the refrigerator. Keep cooked porridge in the refrigerator for three to five days.

content.title: About
content.content: Corn, also called maize (Zea mays), is a cereal grain first domesticated in southern Mexico thousands of years ago. It is now one of the most widely grown crops in the world. Corn is eaten as a vegetable (sweet corn on the cob or as kernels), as a grain, and in products such as cornmeal, polenta, tortillas, popcorn, and corn flour.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Corn was domesticated from a wild grass called teosinte in what is now Mexico.
Botanically, a corn kernel is a fruit called a caryopsis, and corn is also classified as a cereal grain.
An ear of corn usually has an even number of kernel rows, commonly 12 to 18.
Corn comes in many colors, including yellow, white, blue, red, and purple.
Popcorn pops because the water inside the kernel turns to steam and bursts the hard outer layer.

items.title: Provides dietary fiber
items.content: Corn contains fiber, especially when eaten as whole kernels or whole-grain products.

items.title: Contains B vitamins
items.content: Corn provides thiamin and folate, which support energy metabolism and cell function.

items.title: Contains eye-supporting carotenoids
items.content: Yellow corn contains lutein and zeaxanthin, plant pigments associated with eye health.

items.title: Provides minerals
items.content: Corn offers magnesium, potassium, and phosphorus.

items.title: Source of energy
items.content: Corn is rich in carbohydrates, which provide energy.

items.title: Allergic reactions
items.content: Corn allergy is uncommon but can occur.

items.title: Digestive discomfort
items.content: Corn kernels contain insoluble fiber that may cause gas or bloating in some people.

items.title: Carbohydrate content
items.content: Corn is rich in starch, so people monitoring blood sugar should watch portions.

items.title: Mold toxins and niacin
items.content: Poorly stored corn can contain mold toxins such as aflatoxins. Diets that rely heavily on untreated corn can also be low in available niacin.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Sweet corn can be boiled, steamed, grilled, or roasted on the cob, or cut off and added to salads, soups, and sides. Dried corn is ground into cornmeal and flour for porridge, polenta, tortillas, and bread. Popcorn is a popular whole-grain snack when made without a lot of salt or butter.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Fresh sweet corn is best eaten soon after buying; keep it in the refrigerator, ideally in its husk, for a few days, since its sugar turns to starch over time. Kernels can be blanched and frozen. Dried corn, cornmeal, and popcorn should be kept in airtight containers in a cool, dry place.

content.title: About
content.content: The whole wheat hot dog bun (item 2512) is made from 100% whole grain wheat flour, retaining bran and germ for added nutrition compared with standard white buns. It has a soft yet sturdy crumb, a subtle nutty flavor, and is perfect for hot dogs, sausages, or vegetarian fillings.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Whole grain buns retain more fiber, B‑vitamins and minerals than their white counterparts.
These buns became popular in the United States in the early 20th century when whole‑grain flour entered mass production.
Their lower glycemic index means they raise blood sugar more slowly than refined buns.
Often enriched with sunflower or pumpkin seeds for extra crunch and flavor.
Storing them in a vented bag helps keep the crust from becoming soggy.

items.title: High in dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber supports healthy digestion, promotes satiety and helps maintain regular bowel movements.

items.title: Source of B‑vitamins
items.content: Thiamine, riboflavin and niacin aid energy metabolism and support the nervous system.

items.title: Contains essential minerals
items.content: Iron, magnesium and zinc in the bun contribute to blood formation and immune function.

items.title: Low added sugar
items.content: Unlike many white buns, the whole wheat version contains minimal added sugars.

items.title: Heart‑friendly nutrients
items.content: Whole grains provide antioxidants and healthy fats that can help lower LDL cholesterol.

items.title: Wheat/gluten allergy
items.content: People with celiac disease or gluten intolerance should avoid this bun.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Some recipes add salt; those monitoring blood pressure should check the label.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: While more nutritious, the bun still provides calories; portion control is important for weight management.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Warm the bun in an oven or toaster, split it lengthwise and fill with a hot dog, sausage, grilled vegetables or a plant‑based patty. It pairs well with mustard, ketchup, pickles and fresh salad toppings.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep buns in an airtight bag at room temperature for up to 3 days. For longer storage, refrigerate (up to 7 days) or freeze (up to 3 months). Reheat in the oven before serving to restore softness.
